help.intro: A market seller calls out today's prices — apples, bananas, bread, eggs, cheese, potatoes — and you only hear it. Your job is to match each product to its price, which is the most common listening job of daily life: numbers inside real speech, said at real speed. The trick is to hold the pair together: the product name comes first, the price follows within a second or two (… Äpfel … zwei Euro). Prices are said euros first, then cents, with no word for the comma: 2,20 € is 'zwei Euro zwanzig'; 1,10 € is 'ein Euro zehn'. Two prices here are close on purpose — zwei Euro and zwei Euro zehn — so listen to the end of each number. Play it once for the products, once for the prices.
help.tips[0].title: Product, then price
help.tips[0].text: The number always follows the thing it belongs to. Hear 'Bananen', get ready — the next number is theirs.
help.tips[0].check.q: 'Der Käse kostet vier Euro, die Milch kostet zwei Euro.' How much is the cheese?
help.tips[0].check.why: The price follows its product: Käse … vier Euro, then Milch … zwei Euro.
help.tips[1].title: Euros first, cents second, no comma word
help.tips[1].text: 2,20 € = zwei Euro zwanzig. 1,10 € = ein Euro zehn (ein, not eins, before Euro — and 'einen Euro zehn' after kostet is also heard; both are right). Whole euros: zwei Euro, no 's' on Euro.
help.tips[1].check.why: Euros first, then cents, no word for the comma, and Euro never takes an s.
help.tips[2].title: 'billig' is cheap, 'kostet' is costs
help.tips[2].text: Sellers praise: heute billig, nur zwei Euro. 'nur' = only. kosten is the verb you are waiting for — it introduces the price every time. Kilo is a kilogram: ein Kilo Äpfel, no 'of'.
help.tips[2].check.q: 'Heute ist der Käse billig.' What is the seller saying about the cheese?
help.tips[2].check.why: billig means cheap, a seller's favourite word; the actual price comes after kostet.
help.remember[0]: Write the number as you hear it — 'zwei Euro zwanzig' → 2,20 — before the next product starts.
help.remember[1]: kostet / kosten is the bell: the price is the next thing said.
help.exam: Catching one number — a price, a time, a platform — inside a short scene is a standard A1 exam listening text, and daily life at the market and the station.
help.hook: Hear a market seller call out prices and match every product to what it costs, at real speed.
passageTranslation: Good day and welcome to the market! Today the apples are cheap: one kilo costs only two euros. The bananas cost three euros. A loaf of bread costs two euros ten. Would you like eggs too? Ten eggs cost two euros twenty. And the cheese from Holland is cheap today too: one piece costs four euros. The potatoes cost one euro ten. Thank you and have a nice day!
questions[0].explanation: "… ein Kilo kostet nur zwei Euro." — zwei Euro zehn is the bread, drei Euro the bananas.
questions[0].questionTranslation: How much does one kilo of apples cost?
questions[1].explanation: "Die Bananen kosten drei Euro." — the product comes first, its price follows.
questions[2].explanation: "Zehn Eier kosten zwei Euro zwanzig." — zehn is ten.
questions[2].questionTranslation: How many eggs cost two euros twenty?
questions[3].explanation: "… ein Stück kostet vier Euro." — ein Euro zehn is the potatoes.
questions[3].questionTranslation: What does a piece of cheese cost?
questions[4].explanation: "Heute sind die Äpfel billig …" — billig means cheap.
questions[4].questionTranslation: What are the apples like today?
